content.value: Distinguish classes, objects, state, behavior, identity, and references; explain how two variables can refer to one object.

A class describes a kind of object, including the information it stores and the operations it offers. Each object is an instance with identity and instance state. A bank account object might store a balance and provide deposit and getBalance methods. Calling a method asks that receiver object to perform an operation.

A reference variable identifies an object rather than containing the object’s entire state. Assigning one reference to another creates an alias, not an automatic copy of the object. Separate constructor calls can produce objects with equal state but different identities. null means no object is referenced.

first and alias refer to one Counter; second refers to a different Counter. The call through alias changes the shared first object if increment updates its count. It does not change the independent second object. There are three variables but only two constructed objects.
Do not count reference variables as objects. Equal field values do not prove two references identify the same object. Calling an instance method through null fails because no receiver exists.

Draw three boxes for the reference variables and two circles for the objects. Connect first and alias to the same circle. Then predict which connections change if alias = second executes: only alias moves.
